title: The Widow
scripture: Revelation 14:1–3, 4b–5; Psalm 24:1–6; Luke 21:1–4. Additional context: Luke 20:45–47; Matthew 25:31–46.
theme: he extraordinary trust of a poor widow, the faithfulness of those who follow the Lamb, and what Jesus sees that others cannot.
opening: What would it take to give away the very last of what you had, trusting that somehow God would provide? Today's Gospel introduces us to a poor widow who offers two small coins at the Temple. To anyone watching, her gift might have seemed insignificant. But Jesus sees something extraordinary in this woman, something that makes me wonder about the depth of her faith
prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for seeing what others cannot. You know the struggles we carry, the sacrifices we make, and the faith we sometimes find difficult to express. Help me trust You even when I cannot see what lies ahead. Give me the courage to offer You what I can, knowing that You understand the heart behind every gift. Open my eyes to recognize the needs and goodness of those around me, and help our communities reflect Your compassion and care. May my life become a song of faithfulness to You, even in moments when only You can hear it. Amen.
body:
Today's Gospel from Luke 21:1–4 is only four verses long, yet there is so much to consider. Jesus is watching people make their offerings at the Temple in Jerusalem. Wealthy people contribute from their abundance, and then a poor widow approaches and places two small coins into the treasury. Jesus tells His disciples that she has given more than everyone else because, while the others gave from their surplus, she gave everything she had to live on.

At first, I thought about her generosity, but then I began to wonder about her faith. What if this woman knew exactly what she was doing? What if she believed so completely in God's goodness that she could give away her last two coins, trusting that He would somehow care for her? We don't know what was in her heart, but Jesus did. And perhaps that is what makes this encounter so extraordinary.

Understanding the history of the Temple adds another dimension to this story. In Jesus' time, the Temple in Jerusalem was the center of Jewish religious life. It was where people gathered to worship, pray, and offer sacrifices. The widow's two coins were called lepta, among the smallest coins in circulation. Their monetary value was almost nothing, but to this woman, they represented everything she had.

I wonder what brought her to the Temple that day. Had she come to pray? Was she asking God for help? Had she already experienced His goodness in ways that gave her the courage to trust Him again? Scripture doesn't tell us, but I find myself thinking about the strength it must have taken to place those coins into the treasury and walk away.

There is something else worth understanding about the way Luke tells this story. Immediately before this encounter, Jesus warns His disciples about religious leaders who seek recognition and places of honor while exploiting widows. Then He notices this woman giving everything she has. The contrast is difficult to overlook. Throughout the Jewish Scriptures, God commands His people to care for widows, orphans, and those who are vulnerable. The Temple was a place devoted to God, and devotion to God was never meant to be separated from compassion for His people. That remains a responsibility for every community that gathers in His name.

But I don't want to lose sight of the widow herself, because Jesus doesn't. He recognizes her when others might barely notice her. He sees beyond the two coins to the person offering them. He knows her circumstances, her intentions, and the faith that brought her there. He sees what we cannot.

And this brings me to today's first reading from Revelation, which at first seems so different from the Gospel. John describes a vision of the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with 144,000 people who bear His name and the name of His Father. They sing a new hymn before God's throne, a song that no one else can learn except those who have been redeemed. The number 144,000 is commonly understood symbolically, representing the fullness of God's faithful people rather than a literal limit on those who can be saved. These are people who belong to the Lamb and follow Him wherever He goes.

But what especially caught my attention was the song. Why could no one else learn it? Perhaps because it is a song born of redemption, a song understood through belonging to Christ and sharing in His victory. It speaks of a relationship with God that cannot be measured by outward appearances.

And I began thinking about the widow again. We know nothing about her life beyond these few verses. We don't know what she had suffered, what she had prayed for, or how God had accompanied her through her difficulties. But perhaps she, too, carried a song of faith within her heart, one that the people around her could never fully understand. Jesus understood.

There is a beautiful connection between the Lamb in Revelation and Jesus standing in the Temple. The Lamb is Christ, who gave Himself completely for humanity. And here, before His own sacrifice on the Cross, Jesus recognizes a woman who has given everything she has. Her offering cannot be compared with His sacrifice, but it reminds us of what wholehearted trust and self-giving can look like.

Jesus would go on to establish His Church, gathering His followers into a community called to continue His work of love, mercy, and service. The Church is not simply a building or an institution. It is the Body of Christ, made up of people called to recognize His presence in one another. And that calling invites us to notice the person standing before us, especially when their needs or sacrifices are not immediately apparent.

Yesterday, we celebrated Christ the King and heard Jesus tell us that whatever we do for the least among us, we do for Him. Today, we see Him recognize a poor widow whose gift might otherwise have gone unnoticed. I love how the Church's readings can lead us from one day to the next, helping us discover connections we might never have considered.

And perhaps today's readings invite us to think about our own relationship with God. Have we ever trusted Him when we couldn't see what would happen next? Have we ever offered Him something that seemed small to everyone else but required tremendous faith from us?

We may never know what happened to the widow after she left the Temple. I hope she was cared for. I hope she found food, shelter, and kindness. And I hope that the faith she carried into the Temple sustained her in whatever came next.

But one thing we do know is that Jesus saw her. He recognized a gift whose value could never be measured in coins. And perhaps, like those who sing before the Lamb in Revelation, she carried within her a faith that the world could not fully understand.

The widow gave everything she had. Jesus saw everything she was. And sometimes, knowing that God sees us completely is what gives us the courage to trust Him with what comes next.
